import numpy as np

# Custom Colors
CYAN_A = "#00FFFF"
WAREHOUSE_BLUE = "#ADD8E6"
PARIS_MAGENTA = "#FF00FF"

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        self.lecture[1].set_color(COLOR_LABEL)
        
        # Key and Value vectors

        value_vector = Arrow(DOWN, UP, color=COLOR_LABEL, buff=0)

        value_label = Text("Value", font_size=20, color=COLOR_LABEL)

outline.topic: The Library of Weights: How Transformer MLPs Store Facts
outline.target_audience: University students (Computer Science/AI) and tech-savvy learners

sections.title: The Mystery of Model Memory
sections.content: Introduction to the concept: Large Language Models (LLMs) answer questions without looking things up on the internet. We establish that knowledge must be stored within the model's weights. We set the stage for exploring the 'Feed-Forward Network' (MLP) as the primary storage unit.
sections.example: A robot character named 'Lex' is asked: 'What is the capital of France?'. Lex doesn't open a book; he looks deep into his internal circuitry to find 'Paris'.

sections.title: Anatomy Check: Attention vs. MLP
sections.content: Visualizing the Transformer block. Distinguish between the Attention mechanism (the 'Contextual Messenger') and the Multi-Layer Perceptron (the 'Knowledge Warehouse'). Explain that while attention links words, the MLP stores the facts about those words.
sections.example: An animation showing a Transformer block: The Attention layer is a series of telephone wires connecting words, while the MLP is a massive filing cabinet sitting below them.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Key-Value Analogy
sections.content: Introduce the mathematical concept of Key-Value pairs. Explain that the MLP functions like a dictionary. Use a dot product visualization: if an input vector (query) aligns with a 'Key' vector, it unlocks a specific 'Value' vector.
sections.example: A visual of a physical key fitting into a lock. Mathematically, show two arrows (vectors). If they point in the same direction, a light bulb (neuron) turns on.

sections.title: The First Layer: The Pattern Detectors (Keys)
sections.content: Explain the first linear layer ($W_1$) and the activation function (GELU/ReLU). This layer acts as a set of 'detectors.' Each neuron in this layer represents a specific concept or 'Key' that activates when a relevant pattern is present in the input.
sections.example: A grid of 1000 neurons. When the input 'Eiffel Tower' arrives, neuron #402 (the 'French Landmarks' neuron) glows brightly, while others stay dim.

sections.title: The Second Layer: Fact Retrieval (Values)
sections.content: Explain the second linear layer ($W_2$). This layer takes the activation from the first layer and maps it to the output space. These are the 'Values.' If a 'Key' for 'France' is activated, the corresponding 'Value' in $W_2$ adds the 'Paris' vector to the model's hidden state.
sections.example: Neuron #402 pushes a button that releases a cloud of 'Paris-related' particles into the data stream, effectively answering the question.

sections.title: Superposition: A Multi-Dimensional Library
sections.content: Explain how the MLP handles millions of facts simultaneously. Because the vectors are high-dimensional, many 'Key-Value' pairs can exist in the same matrix without interfering with each other, a concept known as superposition.
sections.example: A 3D visualization of a dense galaxy of points. Each point is a fact (e.g., 'Banana-Yellow', 'Mars-Red'). The MLP navigates this space to pull the right color for the right object.

sections.title: Summary: The Weight-Based Encyclopedia
sections.content: Recap the flow: Input -> Key Detection ($W_1$) -> Value Retrieval ($W_2$) -> Knowledge Update. Emphasize that 'learning' is the process of adjusting these weights so the right keys trigger the right values.
sections.example: A final view of Lex the Robot. We see a 'zoom-in' on his CPU where billions of tiny Key-Value pairs are sparking, allowing him to state confidently: 'Paris is the capital of France.'

storyboard.title: The Mystery of Model Memory
lecture_lines: How do AI models remember facts without internet?
Large Language Models store information in their weights.
We'll explore the Feed-Forward Network as a warehouse.
Meet Lex, a robot looking deep into his circuitry.
He finds "Paris" stored within his internal parameters.

storyboard.title: Anatomy Check: Attention vs. MLP
lecture_lines: A Transformer block has two main components.
Attention connects words, while the MLP stores facts.
Think of the MLP as a massive filing cabinet.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Key-Value Analogy
lecture_lines: Think of the MLP as a vast dictionary.
It uses the concept of Key-Value pairs.
An input vector acts as a query key.
If it aligns with a stored key, it activates.
This alignment "unlocks" a specific, meaningful value vector.

storyboard.title: The First Layer: The Pattern Detectors (Keys)
lecture_lines: The first layer consists of concept detectors.
Each neuron represents a specific pattern or key.
These keys identify what the input is about.

storyboard.title: The Second Layer: Fact Retrieval (Values)
lecture_lines: The second layer retrieves the corresponding values.
Activating a key releases its stored data vector.
This adds the specific fact to the model's state.

storyboard.title: Superposition: A Multi-Dimensional Library
lecture_lines: High-dimensional space allows for massive storage capacity.
Millions of facts coexist without interfering with others.
This phenomenon is known as neural superposition.

storyboard.title: Summary: The Weight-Based Encyclopedia
lecture_lines: Models detect keys and retrieve stored values.
Learning is the process of tuning these weights.
Billions of tiny pairs form an internal encyclopedia.
Knowledge is stored directly inside the model's circuitry.
Lex answers correctly because of his internal library.
